blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en:
Search agents adapt their queries, yet fixed search interfaces leave candidate
processing and evidence presentation outside the agent’s direct control.
Our trajectory analysis shows that supporting passages can be retrieved yet
never delivered to the agent; a same-page oracle intervention shows that
changing the returned evidence can reduce subsequent search.
We introduce Programmatic Search Agent (PSA), which makes a local executable
computation over candidates the unit of a search action. PSA unifies a
persistent candidate workspace, flexible primitive composition, and selective
evidence presentation. It incrementally generates program cells that reuse
candidates, execute dependent operations, and select what the agent inspects
next. The runtime resolves specified data dependencies within each cell,
while the agent adapts its search strategy across cells as new evidence arrives.
We compare PSA with the Query-based Agent and Tool-based Agent on InfoSeek-Eval
and BrowseComp-Plus using five policy backbones without task-specific training.
All three interfaces share the search substrate,
and the Tool-based Agent also shares PSA’s primitives and persistent workspace.
Relative to the Query-based Agent, PSA improves macro-averaged task success by
4.00 and 7.56 percentage points on the two benchmarks, respectively;
within-backbone reductions in final-step tokens average 28.3% and 33.9%.
These results support extending agent control beyond query reformulation to
the processing and presentation of retrieved evidence.
Code will be released subject to approval.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Effective search requires more than finding relevant pages: an agent must also
identify and use the evidence they contain. Large language model agents
interleave reasoning and retrieval, reformulating queries to follow leads,
resolve relations, and verify candidate
answers ( Jin et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2026 ) .
Yet a fixed search(query) interface leaves candidate processing outside
the agent’s direct control: the pipeline decides which candidates to retain,
how to rank them, and which passages to return. The agent can revise its query,
but cannot directly revisit those processing choices. This raises our central
question: Should agents only reformulate queries, or also control how
retrieved candidates are processed and presented?

blocks.en:
Our motivating analysis shows why this distinction matters.
In natural Query-based Agent trajectories on
BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , supporting passages can reach
the extraction stage without ever appearing in the agent’s observations;
later search recovers only some of these omissions
(Section 2 ). A controlled oracle intervention
reveals the downstream consequences: for complete omissions, substituting a
supporting passage from the same retrieved page improves task success and
reduces subsequent search decisions in the analyzed cohort. The bottleneck
can therefore lie not only in finding evidence, but also in processing and
presenting evidence already retrieved. These findings motivate giving the
agent control over this part of the search process.

blocks.en:
Exposing individual search operations as tools provides finer control, but
leaves open the appropriate unit of interaction. In our stepwise Tool-based
Agent, independent calls can be batched, whereas dependent stages require
separate model turns to consume preceding outputs. However, a data
dependency need not require a new model judgment : once the agent has specified
how to retrieve, rerank, and extract, the runtime can execute that sequence
before returning control for further reasoning. Building on composable
retrieval pipelines ( Macdonald & Tonellotto, 2020 ) , executable agent
actions ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , and tool planning ( Kim et al., 2024 ) ,
we make a local computation over candidates the unit of a search action
(Figure 1 ).

blocks.en:
Inspired by Perplexity’s Search as Code
architecture ( Perplexity, 2026 ) , we introduce Programmatic Search Agent (PSA) . Conditioned on the task, interaction
history, and a compact description of retained state, PSA incrementally
generates executable program cells. Three mechanisms organize this control:
a persistent candidate workspace retains objects for later reuse; flexible primitive composition combines retrieval, filtering, reranking,
extraction, and deduplication through variables, collection operations, and
bounded control flow; and selective evidence presentation determines
which results become the next observation. For example, a cell can filter and
re-extract from a retained pool without another query, then return selected
source notes while keeping the underlying candidates available. Each new
observation guides the next cell, so the search strategy evolves with the
evidence. A cell may contain a single operation when immediate feedback is
needed, or a dependent chain when its processing logic can already be specified.

We evaluate PSA against the Query-based Agent and Tool-based Agent on

percentage points on the two benchmarks, respectively; within-backbone

and persistent workspace.

blocks.en:
Our contributions are threefold: (i) an empirical analysis of evidence-delivery
limitations in fixed search pipelines, using natural trajectories and a
same-page oracle intervention; (ii) PSA, a search interface that unifies
persistent candidate reuse, flexible primitive composition, and selective
evidence presentation within executable cells; and (iii) a cross-model
evaluation of task success and final-step tokens, complemented by controlled
feedback and decision-budget experiments.

by the search pipeline. We examine the resulting evidence-delivery gap in two steps: trace whether supporting passages available to extraction reach
the agent, then test how changing the returned evidence affects subsequent

blocks.en:
Building on executable code actions ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , PSA makes local
computation over candidates the unit of search. The policy generates an executable program cell that specifies search operations, their data dependencies,
and the output to inspect. The runtime executes the cell over a persistent
workspace, then returns control to the policy to interpret the result and
choose the next action (Figure 3 ). The interface separates
three choices: what candidate state to retain, how to process it, and what
evidence to expose for the next decision. This also separates data dependencies , which the runtime can resolve within a cell, from
decisions that require new model judgment. PSA uses a fixed policy backbone
without task-specific parameter updates.

blocks.en: 3.1 Persistent Candidate Workspace

blocks.en:
Candidate collections persist as addressable objects, not only as text in the
interaction history. The policy can revisit, combine, or reprocess them in
later cells without retrieving them again. It selects each action from the
history and a compact description of this retained state.
Given a question x x and a fixed corpus 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , its state before
interaction t t is s t = ( x , H t , σ ⁡ ( W t ) ) , s_{t}=\bigl(x,H_{t},\sigma(W_{t})\bigr), (1) where H t H_{t} contains previously executed cells and their observations, and W t W_{t} stores retained candidate collections and other cell variables.
The projection σ \sigma describes available variable names, object types, and
collection sizes, making stored objects addressable without exposing all of
their contents. Conditioned on this state, the policy selects either a new
cell or a terminal answer: a t ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) , a t ∈ { Execute ( c ) : c ∈ 𝒞 } ∪ { Finish ( y ) : y ∈ 𝒴 } , a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}),\qquad a_{t}\in\{\operatorname{Execute}(c):c\in\mathcal{C}\}\cup\{\operatorname{Finish}(y):y\in\mathcal{Y}\}, (2) where 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is the supported restricted-Python cell language and 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} the answer space. A Finish \operatorname{Finish} action terminates the
interaction; an Execute \operatorname{Execute} action updates the workspace and returns
an observation. Cells are generated incrementally, so each new observation can
change the next search target, candidate collection, or sequence of operations.
For example, a cell can store a merged evidence pool, and the next cell can
select sources from that pool for a different extraction instruction. The
source objects remain available even when their full contents were not shown

blocks.en:
Following the compositional view of retrieval ( Macdonald & Tonellotto, 2020 ) ,
cells specify operation graphs rather than invoke a mandatory pipeline.
A cell may acquire new candidates, reprocess retained candidates, or combine both,
expressing dependencies and local transformations within one action.
Variable assignment connects primitive outputs to later inputs, while list
operations, bounded loops, and conditionals specify how collections are
processed. Variables can reference results from the current cell or previous
cells. Local collection operations and deduplication require no additional
retrieval or model calls. The following abbreviated excerpt from an executed cell
(Appendix D ) reprocesses a collection retained from the
preceding cell, with no new retrieval: ⬇ focus = filter ( evidence_pool , predicate ) ranked = rerank ( focus ) grounded = extract ( ranked , instruction ) result = {” ids ”: [ r [” passage_id ”] for r in grounded ], ” notes ”: [ r [” note ”][:1600] for r in grounded [:3]]} result # Return this view to the agent ; retain workspace objects . Here, merged was created in the previous cell; predicate and instruction abbreviate the original title condition and relation to
verify, given in Appendix D . The retained pool is filtered
before reranking and extraction, rather than reacquired through another query.
Other cells can instead retrieve and merge new evidence. Collection operations
preserve their specified order; merging pools does not implicitly rerank them.
Supported conditions and bounded loops execute on runtime values without an
intervening policy call. Decisions requiring semantic interpretation of the
returned evidence remain with the policy at the next interaction.

The interface comparison holds search capabilities and candidate-state access

blocks.en:
We use the full evaluation sets of two complementary deep-search benchmarks: BrowseComp-Plus (830 questions), which pairs search-intensive questions
with a fixed webpage corpus and supporting-document annotations ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , and InfoSeek-Eval (300 questions),
the held-out InfoSeek split whose questions are synthesized from hierarchical
research trees and require resolving interdependent constraints ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . For both benchmarks, we assess answer correctness
using the respective official evaluation prompt with GLM-5.3-Flash as the judge model, and report the resulting task success rate.
We report final-step tokens as the complete input messages and output tokens of
the last decision call, averaged over tasks, with the accounting convention
specified in Appendix C .
On BrowseComp-Plus, we additionally
report Recall using its supporting-document annotations.

The Query-based Agent supports multiple parallel search(query) calls
per decision, each executing the fixed funnel for one query.
The Tool-based Agent exposes PSA’s five primitives and persistent alias
workspace, allowing independent calls within one primary stage (retrieve,
rerank, or extract) to be batched with filter and dedupe in a turn; dependent
primary stages require separate turns to consume previously returned aliases.
PSA expresses these dependencies, local collection operations, loops, and
conditionals within one restricted-Python cell. All interfaces use the same
runtime-enforced 20/10/10 per-call limits: retrieval returns at most
20 documents, reranking retains at most 10, and extraction selects at most
10 passages from the first 10 input candidates; smaller sets are permitted.
Each agent receives at most 50 policy decisions per task. This budget counts
model decisions rather than primitive operations, allowing a PSA cell to
compose multiple dependent calls within one decision.
Additional runtime details and the PSA prompt are provided in
Appendix A .

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion and Future Work
blocks.zh: 6. 结论和今后的工作

blocks.en:
Programmatic Search Agent makes executable computations over persistent
candidates the unit of search, giving the agent control over primitive
composition and evidence presentation. Persistent candidates remain available
across cells, allowing new observations to guide their reuse and processing.
Our motivating analysis shows that
fixed processing can omit useful evidence and that changing its presentation
can affect downstream outcomes. Under a shared search substrate, PSA achieves
the highest task success for all five backbones on InfoSeek-Eval and four of
five on BrowseComp-Plus, with the lowest final-step token counts for all five
on both benchmarks. PSA also improves supporting-document Recall over the
Query-based Agent for all five backbones. These results support extending
agent control beyond query reformulation to candidate processing and evidence
presentation.

blocks.en:
A promising next step is to improve search-program generation through
trajectory-based self-distillation. Self-Distillation Policy Optimization
(SDPO) offers a relevant learning principle: use a feedback-conditioned version
of the model to supervise its policy ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) .
The agent could reflect on completed
trajectories, identify effective candidate-processing strategies, and distill
them into reusable search programs. These retrospective summaries and refined
programs could serve as privileged information during training, guiding the
policy to generate effective cells from the context available at each decision.
Candidate programs could be replayed to check executability and task utility
before being used as training targets. A teacher conditioned on the retrospective
guidance could then supervise a student conditioned only on the corresponding
decision-time context.
Distilling this guidance back into the policy would aim to improve primitive
composition and evidence selection without requiring retrospective information
at inference time.

blocks.en:
For each verified passage, we compare its first extraction-candidate event
with its first selection event. Equal events indicate immediate delivery;
a later selection indicates recovery; no selection indicates non-delivery.
Final passage-delivery recall is the per-task fraction of verified available
passages selected at any point. The macro-average covers the 92 tasks with
verified passages, while passage-level proportions pool their 370 passages.
The other 36 tasks are excluded from recall averages. This passage-ID accounting
does not measure semantic observation coverage. Later selection alone does not
establish query reformulation; extraction-event order is not decision order.
Confidence intervals use 20,000 task-cluster bootstrap replicates,
retaining all passages within each sampled task and resampling separately
within the two source cohorts.

evidence, so its total entry count is not held fixed.
